summary: This unit teaches you to buy the materials for electrical jobs so that the right goods arrive at the right time and price, within the budget. You will learn to work out quantities from drawings, describe materials exactly, get and compare quotations, raise approved purchase orders, receive and check deliveries, match invoices before payment, and keep stock, records and your dealings with suppliers honest.

blocks.p: At Level 3 you do more than collect materials. You work out what a job needs, choose where to buy it, commit the firm's money and answer for the result. Poor purchasing shows up on site as wrong breakers, workers waiting for cable, fake goods that fail inspection and jobs that lose money. This unit is for Level 3 trainees who will run the purchasing for jobs or for a small contractor's store, and who will supervise others who order and receive goods.

blocks.h: What you must be able to do

head: Task
What it looks like on the job
rows: Do a take-off from the drawings, specification and schedules; add a sensible waste allowance; round up to pack sizes; check what is already in stock.
Write each item with its type, size, rating, poles or cores, insulation, standard and part number, quantity and unit, so it can only be read one way.
Use approved suppliers, send the same written enquiry to each, and get written quotations for larger orders.
Compare price, discounts, GCT, delivery, lead time, terms, quality and warranty, and write down why one offer was chosen.
Work out costs and control the budget
Calculate totals, discounts and the J$ cost of imports; keep a running total of orders against the materials budget; report early when costs rise.
Turn a requisition into a numbered purchase order, signed by a person allowed to approve that amount.
Order long-lead items early, call off bulky goods in stages, and keep a schedule of order and delivery dates.
Check goods against the order and delivery note, read the markings, record shortages and damage before signing, and handle returns and credit notes.
Match the order, the goods-received record and the invoice, and query any difference before the firm pays.
Set reorder levels, store goods safely, count stock, and keep purchase records for costing, warranty claims and audits.
Refuse gifts that could sway you, declare conflicts of interest, keep prices confidential and follow the firm's purchasing rules.

flow: A need appears: a job's take-off, or a stock item at its reorder level
Requisition: the internal request to buy, with the job number
Enquiry and quotations from approved suppliers
Compare the offers, choose, and record the reason
Purchase order, approved within the right limit
Delivery received, checked and recorded
Invoice matched against the order and the goods received
Supplier paid on the agreed terms
Records filed; the supplier's performance noted

blocks.p: Each step leaves a document. Together they show what was needed, what was agreed, what arrived and what was paid. When one document is missing, mistakes and dishonesty can pass unnoticed.

ul: The electrical code used in Jamaica is based on the US National Electrical Code (NEC), so most goods sold here are made to North American standards. Wire is usually sized in **AWG** (12 AWG, 10 AWG) and sold by the foot or in **500 ft rolls (about 152 m)**; PVC conduit often comes in **10 ft lengths (about 3 m)**. Some goods are metric (mm² cable, 20 mm conduit). Always check the supplier's unit before you order.
Trade prices are quoted in **J$**, often **excluding GCT**. Imported goods may be priced in **US$**, so their J$ cost moves with the exchange rate.
Much of what is sold is imported, so **lead times** for anything unusual (large breakers, switchboards, transfer switches, special light fittings) can be weeks or months.

A new or altered installation must pass inspection before JPS connects it; this is overseen by the Government Electrical Regulator (GER). Wrong, fake or uncertified materials can fail that inspection, so careful buying protects the whole job.

blocks.note: In the **hurricane season (June to November)**, and especially after a storm, cable, breakers, generators and transfer switches can sell out quickly and prices can rise. For jobs at that time of year, order critical items early and keep a little more safety stock of common items.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: Read the sections in order: they follow a purchase from the drawing to the payment. Work through every example with a calculator. Then try the practice test and read each explanation, even when your answer was right. Your instructor will give you the Centre's own forms and approval rules.

sections.title: Working out what to buy: the take-off

blocks.p: A **take-off** (also called a bill of materials or materials schedule) lists every item a job needs, with its quantity, taken off the drawings and documents. The enquiry, the order and the budget are all built on it, so an error here is repeated all the way through.

head: Document
What it gives you
rows: Positions of outlets, switches, lights, boards and equipment; cable routes; the scale of the drawing.
The type and quality of every item: cable type, accessory range, breaker type, conduit material, the standards to meet.
Schedules (circuit, panel and light fitting schedules)
Each circuit's cable size and breaker rating; the board's ways; fitting types and numbers.
Bill of quantities from the client, if there is one
A list to price against. Check it against the drawings: it can be wrong.
What the drawings do not show: wall types, ceiling heights, routes round beams, existing equipment to be reused.

blocks.note: Check the **revision letter or date** on every drawing, and ask the designer which revision is current. Buying from an old revision is one of the commonest and costliest purchasing errors.
blocks.label: Remember

ol: Work room by room or circuit by circuit. Mark each item on a copy of the drawing with a highlighter as you count it, so nothing is counted twice or missed.
Count the accessories: switches, outlets, light points, boxes, blanks, the board and its breakers.
Measure each cable and conduit run with a scale rule, using the drawing's scale. At **1:100**, 1 cm on the drawing is 1 m on site; at **1:50**, 1 cm is 0.5 m.

Add what a plan cannot show: the **drops** down the wall to each switch or outlet, the rise to the ceiling at the board, and the extra length needed at each end to make off the connections (often about 0.3 m per end; follow your firm's practice).
Total the length for each cable type and size separately. Do the same for conduit and trunking.
Add the fittings that go with each run: couplings, bends, straps or saddles, boxes, connectors, fixings and consumables such as solvent cement, tape and cable ties.

blocks.p: **Worked example.** A cable run measures 9.6 cm on a 1:50 drawing, so on site it is 9.6 × 0.5 = 4.8 m. At the board the cable comes down 1.0 m from the ceiling; at the switch it drops 1.4 m. Allow 0.3 m at each end for connections. Length = 4.8 + 1.0 + 1.4 + 0.3 + 0.3 = **7.8 m**.

Add a **waste allowance** for offcuts, mistakes and routes that turn out longer than drawn. Many firms add about **5 to 10%** to cable and conduit; use your firm's figure. Then **round up** to the pack size the supplier sells: you cannot buy 2.4 cartons.

blocks.note: **Round up once, at the end.** If you round each room's cable up to a whole roll, you buy far too much. Total the whole job first, add the allowance once, then round up to whole packs.
blocks.label: Tip

ul: Check the firm's store for items already held, including part-used rolls and drums, and reserve them for the job on the stock record so they are not used elsewhere.
Check whether the client is supplying any items themselves (free-issue materials), such as light fittings they have already bought.
Check whether the specification allows anything from the old installation to be reused.

blocks.p: At Level 3 you answer for the take-off even when a trainee did part of it. Check each part of a junior's take-off, or a good sample of their counts and measurements, before anything is ordered, and correct errors with an explanation. A useful cross-check is to compare the totals with a similar job done before: a big difference is not proof of an error, but it tells you where to look.

A supplier can only send what you describe. A vague order line lets the supplier choose, and you may get the wrong item, a poorer quality or a fake. Write each line so that **only one product** fits it.

head: Item
What the order line must state
rows: Type and insulation (for example THHN/THWN, NM-B, UF, armoured), conductor size (AWG or mm²), number of cores, copper or aluminium, insulation colour, voltage and temperature rating, quantity and unit (m, ft, rolls, drums).
The panel they must fit (the make and type on the panel label), number of poles, current rating, interrupting (breaking) capacity in kA, any GFCI or AFCI function, quantity.
Rating (15 A or 20 A; 110 V or 220 V pattern), type (duplex, GFCI, tamper-resistant, weather-resistant), colour, and the range named in the specification.
Material (PVC, EMT, rigid steel), size, wall type (for example schedule 40 PVC), length per piece, and matching fittings.
Model or part number, wattage, colour temperature, voltage, driver type, and the IP rating for outdoor or wet places.
Product name and container size; ask for the safety data sheet (SDS).

head: Vague (do not use)
Exact
rows: 20 × single-pole 20 A plug-in breakers, of the type listed on the label of panel L1, 10 kA
3 rolls × 500 ft, 12 AWG THHN/THWN copper, black, 600 V
23 × 3/4 in PVC conduit, schedule 40, 10 ft lengths, grey
40 × LED panel 600 × 600 mm, 40 W, 4000 K, 110–220 V driver, part no. as in the fitting schedule

ul: **Same size, different use.** 12 AWG copper comes as THHN single conductors for conduit, NM-B sheathed cable for dry indoor use, UF for direct burial, and armoured cable. They are not interchangeable: the wrong one can be against the code for that location and fail inspection.

**Breakers must suit the panel.** A breaker of another make may clip onto the busbar but not be listed (approved) for that panel. It may grip poorly, overheat and void the panel's listing. Order the type named on the panel label, or one that its maker states is classified for that panel.

**Breaking capacity.** A breaker's interrupting rating (kA) must be at least the fault current at that board, which the designer states. A cheaper breaker with a lower kA rating may fail violently on a short circuit.
**Part numbers remove doubt** where several versions look alike, such as light fittings with different drivers, beam angles or colour temperatures.

blocks.note: **Fake (counterfeit) electrical goods** are sold in the Caribbean as elsewhere. A fake breaker may not trip; fake cable may have less copper than marked and thin insulation. Warning signs: a price far below every other supplier, poor printing or misspelled markings, missing or odd certification marks, and goods that feel light. Buy from approved suppliers, look for a recognised certification mark (such as UL or CSA on goods made to North American standards), and quarantine anything doubtful instead of using it.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.h: Substitutes and changes to the specification

blocks.p: When the specified item is out of stock, suppliers often offer an 'equivalent', and clients sometimes ask for something cheaper. You may not accept a change on your own: the specification is the designer's and the client's decision.

flow: Get the full details of the offered item: data sheet, ratings, standard and certification
Compare it with the specification, point by point
Refer it to the designer or supervisor with your comparison
Where it changes the client's job, the client agrees in writing
Record the approved change on the order and in the job file

blocks.note: If a proposed substitute is smaller, lower-rated or of a different type, the designer must check that it still meets the code, for example that a smaller cable still suits its breaker and load. Never accept 'near enough' on cable size, breaker rating or breaking capacity.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: An **approved supplier** (or preferred supplier) is one the firm has checked and agreed to buy from. A list of approved suppliers stops staff buying from unknown sources, and makes it easier to hold suppliers to account.

head: What the firm checks
Why it matters
rows: Quality: genuine, certified goods that meet the specification
Poor or fake goods fail, start fires and fail inspection.
Reliability: correct, complete and on-time deliveries
Late or wrong deliveries leave workers idle and delay the job.
Price and terms: trade discounts, credit account, payment terms
They affect the job's cost and the firm's cash flow.
Whether the supplier can provide what you need when you need it.
After-sales support: returns, warranty claims, technical help
Faulty goods must be replaced quickly.
Business details: registered business, TRN, GCT registration
Needed for proper tax invoices and the firm's records.

blocks.p: Review the list regularly. Keep a simple record of each delivery: on time or late, correct or with errors, damaged or not, and how complaints were handled. That record, not friendship or habit, decides who stays on the list.

head: Document
What it is
rows: Your written request to each supplier, listing exactly what you need, the quantities, the delivery place and date, and the date you need the quotation by.
The supplier's general prices for anyone. They may change without notice. Useful for estimates, but not a firm offer for your order.
The supplier's written offer to supply the stated items at stated prices and terms, for a stated time (for example 'valid 30 days').
A bill sent before the goods are released, common for imports and cash-in-advance sales.

ul: Send the **same** enquiry to every supplier, so the quotations can be compared fairly.
Ask each to state: unit prices, discounts, whether GCT is included, delivery charge, lead time, payment terms, how long the offer is valid, warranty, and any substitutes offered.
For larger orders, many firms require **three written quotations**. Public bodies must follow the government's procurement rules. Follow your firm's limits.
Check the **validity** of a quotation. Once it has expired, the supplier is no longer bound by its prices, so confirm them again before you order.
Keep every supplier's prices **confidential**. Never tell one supplier what another quoted so that it can 'beat' the price: it is unfair, and honest suppliers stop quoting.

blocks.p: Put the quotations side by side in a table. First check that each one quotes exactly what you asked for, and mark any substitutes. Then compare on the **same basis**: all prices before GCT (or all including it), with discounts taken off and delivery added.

The lights are needed in 3 weeks. C is cheapest but cannot deliver in time and shows no certification, so it is not suitable. A is cheaper than B once the discount and the delivery charge are counted, arrives in time and has the same warranty: A gives the best value. Write that reason on the comparison sheet.

blocks.note: **Best value is not the lowest price.** An item that arrives late, fails early, does not meet the specification or fails inspection costs far more than the few dollars saved on the quotation.
blocks.label: Remember

head: Choice
What to weigh up
rows: A full drum or roll, or cut lengths
A drum is cheaper per metre, but poor value if most of it will sit unused for months, tying up money and space. Some suppliers charge a deposit on drums and refund it when they are returned.
A lower unit price, but only worth it if you have the storage, the cash and a real use for the stock.
Before a large order of light fittings or accessories, ask for a sample to check quality, finish and fit.
Imported goods may be cheaper or better, but lead time, exchange rate, freight and customs add cost and risk.
Splitting an order can save money but adds deliveries, invoices and checking. Some items, such as all the breakers for one board, are best from one source.

sections.title: Costs, GCT, imports and the budget

head: Calculation
How
Example
rows: Pack price ÷ length in the pack
J$41 900 ÷ 152 m = about J$276 a metre
Line totals after discounts, plus delivery
Taxable total × the current GCT rate
Shown as a separate line on the order and the invoice

blocks.p: **GCT** (General Consumption Tax) is added to most goods sold in Jamaica. A price marked **exclusive** of GCT ('excl. GCT', 'plus GCT') still has the tax to be added; an **inclusive** price already contains it. Check which one every quotation uses before you compare, and use the current rate given by your accounts office, because the rate can change. A business registered for GCT can normally claim back the GCT it pays on business purchases, which is one reason the accounts office needs proper tax invoices that show the supplier's TRN and the GCT as a separate amount.

head: Term
Meaning
rows: Pay the full amount within 30 days of the invoice date.
Take 2% off if you pay within 10 days; otherwise the full amount is due within 30 days.
Cash in advance, or against a pro forma invoice
Pay before the goods are released; common for imports and new customers.
The supplier lets the firm buy now and pay on agreed terms, up to a credit limit.

blocks.p: **Example.** An invoice for J$86 000 is on terms of 2/10, net 30. Paying within 10 days saves 2% × 86 000 = **J$1 720**. Whether that is worth doing depends on the firm's cash, so tell the accounts office about such discounts so that they are not missed.
The **landed cost** is what an imported item really costs by the time it is in your store. The supplier's US$ price is only the start.

flow: The supplier's price in US$
× the exchange rate when you pay (J$ per US$1)
+ freight and insurance to Jamaica
+ customs duty and import taxes, including GCT on imports
+ customs broker, port and handling charges
+ local delivery to the store or site
= the landed cost in J$

blocks.p: **Example (made-up rate).** A transfer switch costs US$2 400. At J$156 to US$1, that is 2 400 × 156 = **J$374 400**, before any freight, duty, taxes or fees. The exchange rate may move between the quotation and the payment, so get the J$ cost confirmed, and allow a margin, before you commit the firm.
The job's estimate contains a **materials budget**. Your job is to buy what the job needs within it, and to warn early when that will not be possible.

ul: Break the budget down by main item or stage: cable, containment, accessories, board and breakers, light fittings.
Keep a **running total** of approved orders (the committed cost), including delivery, and compare it with the budget for each item.
Check every invoice against its order, so that extra charges do not slip in.
Control waste: order from an accurate take-off, issue materials against job cards, and return unused items to the store or the supplier.

When costs start to rise, find the cause (price rises, waste, theft, extra work) and tell your supervisor **early, with figures**. Extra work the client asks for is priced as a **variation** and charged to the client, not hidden in the budget.

blocks.p: The cable line is forecast to go 5.7% over (24 000 ÷ 420 000 × 100). That is the time to act, while choices can still be made, not when the last roll has been bought.

sections.title: Requisitions, purchase orders, approval and timing

blocks.p: A **requisition** (purchase requisition) is the internal request to buy. The person who needs the goods, such as the job supervisor or the storekeeper, raises it with what is needed, how many, by when and for which job. The purchaser then gets prices and raises the **purchase order (PO)**: the firm's formal instruction to the supplier.

head: What the PO shows
Why it matters
rows: The firm's name, address and TRN, and a unique PO number
The number links the order, delivery note and invoice so that they can be matched.
The supplier's name and the quotation reference
The agreed prices and terms apply.
Each line: description, size, rating, part number, quantity, unit, unit price, line total
The right item arrives at the agreed price.
Subtotal, discount, delivery, GCT shown separately, total
The cost can be checked against the budget and the invoice.
Delivery address, date needed, site contact and phone
Someone is there to receive and check the goods.
The cost is charged to the right job.
Both sides know when payment is due.
Signature of an authorised person, and the date
The firm controls who commits its money.

blocks.p: Most firms set **approval limits** (delegated authority). For example, a purchaser may sign orders up to a set amount, and anything larger goes to a manager. The limits protect the firm and the purchaser.

ul: Never split one purchase into several smaller orders, or ask a supplier to split its invoice, to keep each part under your limit. That defeats the control, and auditors look for it.
If the cost of an approved order rises (a price increase, extra items), get it approved again at the new total.
An order placed by phone or e-mail must still be backed by a numbered PO, so that it can be matched later.
Many firms also keep **ordering and paying apart**: the person who places orders does not also approve payments. This makes errors and fraud much harder to hide.

blocks.p: Small urgent items, such as a box of wire connectors from a hardware store near the site, may be bought with petty cash or a company card, within the firm's limit. Always bring back an itemised receipt showing the shop, the date, the items, the prices and the GCT, and write the job number on it. Without it, the cost cannot be charged to the job or the GCT claimed back.

blocks.h: Timing: lead times and the job programme

blocks.p: **Lead time** is the time from placing an order to receiving the goods. Plan each purchase backwards from the date the item is needed on site.

flow: The date it is needed on site, from the job programme
minus the supplier's lead time (and customs clearance for imports)
minus a safety margin for delays
minus the time needed for quotations and approval
= the latest date to start buying

blocks.p: **Example.** A special board is needed on site in week 7 of a job. Its lead time is 6 weeks; you allow 1 week's margin and 1 week to get quotations and approval. 7 − 6 − 1 − 1 = week −1: you must start buying a week **before** the job begins, as soon as the design is approved.

ul: **Long-lead items** (switchboards, large breakers, generators, transfer switches, imported fittings) are ordered first.

**Bulky, common items** (cable, conduit, boxes) are **called off** in stages: one order at an agreed price, delivered in parts a few days before each stage of work. This saves site space and cuts theft, weather damage and double handling.
Keep an order and delivery schedule, and check it each week against progress. If the programme moves, move the deliveries.

head: Item
Needed on site
Lead time
Order by
Delivery
rows: Call-off 1 in week 1; call-off 2 in week 4

sections.title: Receiving deliveries and dealing with problems

ul: Have a copy of the purchase order ready; the delivery note alone tells you only what the supplier says it sent.
Make sure someone who can check the goods is there at the agreed time.
Clear a safe unloading area on firm ground, away from traffic, with a trolley, sack truck or forklift for heavy drums.
Plan where the goods will be stored: secure, dry and out of the way.

flow: Check the delivery note against the PO: supplier, PO number, items
Count every item; open cartons where you can
Read the markings: size and type printed on the cable, breaker rating and type, part numbers
Look for damage: crushed cartons, dented drums, broken fittings, wet goods
Check that any SDS and certificates have come with the goods
Write every problem on the delivery note, then sign
Fill in the goods-received note (GRN) and update the stock records

blocks.note: Sign only for what you have actually checked. If you cannot check everything while the driver waits, write that on the note in the way your firm allows (for example 'received unchecked'), check at once, and report problems to the supplier the same day. Never sign a clean note for goods you have not seen.
blocks.label: Tip

head: Problem
What to do
rows: Write the shortage on the delivery note before signing and tell the purchaser. The supplier sends the balance or credits it.
Wrong item (for example 12 AWG instead of 10 AWG, or 16 A breakers instead of 20 A)
Do not use it, even if someone says it 'will do'. Note it, tag it, keep it apart, and arrange a return and the correct item.
Note the damage, take photos, tag the items and keep them apart; claim a replacement or a credit.
Note it. Do not keep goods you did not order unless the purchaser agrees, or the firm may be billed for them.
Treat it as a wrong item until the designer approves it in writing.
Ask the supplier for it before the product is used; it can usually be sent by e-mail at once.
Quarantine them, report them, and do not use them.

blocks.h: Returns, credit notes and debit notes

ul: A **returns note** goes with goods sent back, quoting the PO and delivery note numbers and the reason.
A **credit note** from the supplier reduces what the firm owes, for example for returned, faulty or short-delivered goods that were already invoiced.
Some firms send a **debit note** to tell a supplier of an amount they are claiming back.
File the paperwork with the job's purchase records, and check that each credit appears on the supplier's next statement.

blocks.p: PVC solvent cement and primer, contact cleaner, cable-pulling lubricant and some paints are hazardous. Each must be covered by a **safety data sheet (SDS)**, which gives the hazards, safe storage, PPE, first aid and what to do about a spill. Store flammable products closed and labelled, away from heat and sparks, in a ventilated place, and keep the SDS where workers can read it.

blocks.note: Lift safely when you unload: bend your knees, keep the load close, and use a trolley or get help for heavy boxes. A full drum of cable can weigh well over 100 kg: move it with the right equipment, chock it, and never stand on the downhill side of a drum on a slope.
blocks.label: Safety

sections.title: Paying suppliers, records and stock control

blocks.p: Before any supplier is paid, three records are checked against each other:

head: Document
What it shows
rows: What the firm agreed to buy, and at what price
Goods-received note (or the signed delivery note)
What actually arrived and was accepted
What the supplier is asking to be paid

blocks.p: Items, quantities and prices must agree on all three. Any difference is **queried with the supplier before payment**, and only the correct amount is paid. This protects the firm from paying for goods it never received, wrong prices, double invoices and goods that were sent back.

**Example.** PO 3318 was for 10 rolls at J$41 900. The GRN shows 9 rolls accepted and 1 returned damaged. The invoice charges 10 rolls at J$42 500, a total of J$425 000. The firm pays for 9 rolls at the PO price, 9 × 41 900 = **J$377 100** before GCT, once the supplier sends a corrected invoice or a credit note.

head: Record
Why it is kept
rows: Show why the supplier was chosen and that the process was fair.
Show who committed the money, and within what limit.
Delivery notes, GRNs, returns and credit notes
Show what arrived and what went back.
Needed for the accounts, GCT returns and audits.
Needed for warranty claims and for the inspection of the installation.
Help decide who stays on the approved list.

blocks.p: File them by job and by supplier, on paper or electronically, for as long as the firm's policy and the tax rules require. When a batch of LED drivers fails a few months after fitting, the purchase records and the warranty terms are what get the firm free replacements.
A contractor's store holds common items so that jobs do not wait for every small purchase. Stock ties up money and space, so the aim is enough, not too much.

head: Term
Meaning
rows: Stock card, bin card or stock spreadsheet
The record of each item: what came in, what went out (and to which job), and the balance.
How many are used in a day or a week, on average.
Extra stock kept to cover late deliveries or unusually high use.
The balance at which you order more: usage during the lead time + safety stock.
How many to order each time, set by usage, pack sizes, price breaks and space.
Issue the oldest stock first, so nothing ages on the shelf.
A physical count, compared with the records.

blocks.p: **Example.** The store issues about 12 duplex outlets a working day. The supplier delivers in 4 working days, and the firm keeps 20 as safety stock. Reorder level = 12 × 4 + 20 = **68**. When the stock card shows 68 or fewer, reorder.

ul: Issue materials only against a job card or requisition, so that every item is charged to a job.

Count stock regularly. A difference between the count and the record may be an issue not written down, a recording error, damage or theft. Find out which, correct the record with approval, and fix the cause.
Review **slow-moving** items. Stop reordering things that are rarely used, and use up, return or sell old stock before it is damaged or out of date.
Cable drums on chocks or a drum rack, off the ground and under cover: sunlight breaks down sheaths, and water gets into cut ends. Seal cut ends with tape or end caps.
Conduit and trunking flat on racks, not leaning in corners.
Small parts in labelled bins by size and rating, with heavy items on the lower shelves.
Breakers and electronic items in their boxes, dry and secure.
Flammable chemicals in a ventilated cabinet away from heat, with the SDS on file.
High-value items (copper cable, breakers, tools) locked away: copper theft is common.

sections.title: Ethics, waste and leading the purchasing

blocks.p: A purchaser spends the firm's money and must act in the firm's interest, not their own. Suppliers compete for orders, and some will try to win them unfairly.

head: Situation
What to do
rows: A supplier offers a gift, cash, a trip or a 'commission' for orders
Refuse anything that could affect your choice, or look as if it does, and tell your manager. Follow the firm's gift policy for small items such as a calendar.
A friend or relative owns or works for a supplier
Declare it to your manager, and let someone else make or check the choice.
A supplier asks what a rival quoted
Do not tell them. Ask every supplier for its best offer on the same terms, at the same time.
You are asked to split an order or change a date to get round a limit
Refuse, and refer it to the person who sets the limits.
A supplier offers to invoice for goods it did not deliver, or to bill 'extras' to another job
Refuse and report it: this is fraud.
You make a mistake on an order
Own it, tell your supervisor and put it right quickly.

blocks.note: Bribery and fraud are crimes, and buying for a public body is controlled by strict procurement rules. Even when nothing illegal happens, a purchaser who is seen to favour a supplier loses the trust of the firm and of honest suppliers.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: An accurate take-off is the biggest saving of all: less over-ordering and fewer leftovers.
Ask suppliers for less packaging, and for bulk packs instead of many small ones where they will be used.
Return empty cable drums and reels where the supplier has a return or deposit scheme.
Keep useful offcuts and part rolls in the store, labelled with size and length, for the next job.
Choose products that last and can be repaired or recycled.

blocks.h: Leading the purchasing on a job

ul: Agree with the job supervisor who may raise requisitions, who places orders and who receives goods on site.
Teach junior staff and trainees what to check on delivery, and give them a copy of the order, not just the delivery note.
Check a sample of each person's take-off and receiving work, and correct errors with an explanation.
Hold a short weekly review: orders placed, deliveries due, problems, and the budget position.
Report to the job manager: what has been bought, what is due, the risks (late items, price rises) and the budget forecast.

blocks.note: Write down the reason for every important decision: why this supplier, why this quantity, why the order went in on that date. A short note now saves a long argument later.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Tick each statement only when you can do it without looking at the notes.

ul: I can do a take-off from the latest drawings, schedules and specification, measuring runs to scale and adding drops and connection lengths.
I can add a waste allowance once, convert units (feet and metres) and round up to the supplier's pack sizes.
I can write an order line that describes an item so exactly that only one product fits it.
I can explain why breakers must suit the panel and why cable type, not just size, must be stated.
I can spot the warning signs of fake goods and say what to do with doubtful items.
I can handle a substitute or a cheaper alternative without changing the specification on my own.
I can send a fair enquiry and compare quotations on the same basis: price, discount, GCT, delivery, lead time, terms, quality and warranty.
I can calculate line totals, discounts, early-payment savings, price per metre and the J$ cost of an imported item.
I can explain the landed cost of an import and why the exchange rate is a risk.
I can keep a running total of orders against the materials budget and report a forecast overspend early.
I can raise a purchase order with all its parts and follow the firm's approval limits.
I can work back from the date an item is needed to the latest date to order it.
I can receive a delivery, record problems before signing, and deal with returns and credit notes.
I can carry out a three-way match before a supplier is paid.
I can set a reorder level, explain FIFO and deal with a stock count that does not match the records.
I can store materials and chemicals safely and keep the right purchase records.
I can act honestly with suppliers and lead others who order and receive goods.

head: Item
What it is
rows: Need × (1 + waste allowance), then rounded up to whole packs
1 cm on the drawing = 0.5 m and 1 m on site
Usage per day (or week) × lead time in days (or weeks) + safety stock
US$ price × exchange rate, then add freight, duty, taxes and fees
Date needed − lead time − margin − time for quotes and approval
Forecast − budget; as a percentage, variance ÷ budget × 100

terms: Approval limit
The largest order a person is allowed to sign for; larger orders go to someone with a higher limit.
Approved supplier
A supplier the firm has checked and agreed to buy from.
Call-off order
One order at agreed prices, delivered in parts when each stage of work needs them.
Credit note
A supplier's document that reduces what the firm owes, for example after a return.
Delivery note
The list of goods handed over with a delivery, signed by the person receiving them.
Enquiry (RFQ)
A written request to suppliers to quote for exactly stated goods.
Exclusive / inclusive of GCT
A price with GCT still to be added / a price that already contains GCT.
FIFO
First in, first out: issuing the oldest stock first.
GCT
General Consumption Tax, added to most goods sold in Jamaica, at the current rate.
Goods-received note (GRN)
The firm's own record of what arrived and was accepted.
Landed cost
The full cost of an imported item in your store: price, exchange, freight, duty, taxes and fees.
Lead time
The time from placing an order to receiving the goods.
Purchase order (PO)
The firm's numbered, approved instruction to a supplier to supply goods.
Quotation
A supplier's written offer to supply stated goods at stated prices and terms, for a stated time.
Reorder level
The stock balance at which more is ordered.
Requisition
The internal request to buy, raised by the person who needs the goods.
Safety stock
Extra stock kept to cover late deliveries or high use.
Take-off
A list of all the materials a job needs, with quantities, taken from the drawings and documents.
Three-way match
Checking that the order, the goods-received record and the invoice agree before paying.
Variation
A change or extra work asked for by the client, priced and charged separately.
Waste allowance
An extra percentage added to a quantity for offcuts and errors.

c1.title: Rewiring a guest house in Treasure Beach
c1.text: Kevon Walters, a Level 3 electrician, is preparing the materials for rewiring an eight-room guest house in Treasure Beach, St Elizabeth. The designer's drawings are revision C at a scale of 1:50; the owner has also handed him a copy of revision B. The take-off gives 420 m of 12 AWG THHN in black for the outlet circuits. The firm adds 10% for waste, and the supplier sells this wire only in 500 ft rolls (about 152 m). The new panel is a 24-way board of one make, and the supplier offers cheaper 20 A breakers of another make 'that clip in just the same'.

c2.title: LED panels for a high school in Port Maria
c2.text: Tamara Gayle buys materials for a contractor that will replace 120 fluorescent fittings with LED panels at a high school in Port Maria, St Mary, during the summer holiday. The work starts in 4 weeks. Supplier A (approved) quotes J$6 800 each excluding GCT, with 5% off orders over 100 panels, free delivery, a 1-week lead time and a 3-year warranty. Supplier B (approved) quotes J$7 600 each including GCT, plus J$12 000 delivery, a 2-week lead time and a 3-year warranty. Supplier C, not on the approved list, quotes J$5 900 each 'all in', with a 6-week lead time; its sample panel carries no certification mark.

c3.title: An imported switchboard for a Montego Bay supermarket
c3.text: Tanisha Morgan is the purchaser for a contractor fitting out a new supermarket in Montego Bay, St James. The main switchboard must be built overseas: it is priced at US$18 500, with a lead time of 10 weeks from order, plus about 1 week to clear customs. It is needed on site in week 9 of the 16-week programme, and the firm allows 1 week's margin on imports. Tanisha may approve orders up to J$1 500 000; larger orders go to the contracts manager. For this exercise, use J$157 to US$1.

c4.title: A delivery to a hotel extension in Negril
c4.text: Omari Reid, a Level 3 trainee acting as site supervisor, receives a delivery at a hotel extension in Negril, Westmoreland. Purchase order 5520 lists 6 rolls of 10 AWG THHN (black, 500 ft), 40 single-pole 20 A breakers for panel P2, and 4 tins of PVC solvent cement. The delivery note lists the same. Omari finds that one roll is printed '12 AWG', only 38 breakers have come, and there is no safety data sheet for the solvent cement. The driver is in a hurry and asks him to sign straight away.

c5.title: The store of a contractor in Spaldings
c5.text: Sanya Grant runs the store of an electrical contractor in Spaldings, Clarendon. The store issues about 9 single-pole 20 A breakers a week; the supplier delivers in 3 weeks, and the firm keeps 10 as safety stock. At this month's stocktake Sanya counts 31 of these breakers, but the stock card shows 36. She also finds a drum of 6 AWG cable that has not been used for 14 months, while the stock list still says to reorder it when it runs low.

questions.q: How many 500 ft rolls of the black 12 AWG wire should Kevon order?
o: 3 rolls
4 rolls
5 rolls
6 rolls
questions.why: 420 m plus 10% is 462 m. One roll is about 152.4 m, so 462 ÷ 152.4 = 3.03, which rounds up to 4 rolls. Three rolls (457 m) would be just short; 5 rolls comes from wrongly using 100 m rolls.

questions.q: One run measures 7.2 cm on the 1:50 drawing. It drops 1.4 m at the switch and 1.0 m at the panel, and Kevon allows 0.3 m at each end for connections. How long is the run?
questions.why: At 1:50, 1 cm is 0.5 m, so 7.2 cm is 3.6 m. Add 1.4 + 1.0 for the drops and 0.3 + 0.3 for the ends: 3.6 + 2.4 + 0.6 = 6.6 m. Forgetting the drops gives 4.2 m; reading the drawing as 1:100 gives 10.2 m.

questions.q: What should Kevon do about the cheaper breakers of another make?
o: Accept them, because they have the same 20 A rating and fit
Order the type named on the panel label, or one classified for it
Accept them, but fit them only on the lighting circuits
Accept them if the supplier will give a longer warranty
questions.why: A breaker that clips onto a panel is not the same as one listed for it: it may grip the busbar poorly, overheat and void the panel's listing, and it can fail inspection. Buy the type the panel label names, or one its maker states is classified for that panel.

questions.q: The owner's revision B copy shows two more outlets in the kitchen than revision C. What should Kevon do before the order is placed?
o: Order for revision B, since extra outlets will be useful anyway
Order the larger of the two counts, to be safe either way
Order for revision C and ignore the owner's older copy
Confirm with the designer which revision is current, then order
questions.why: Buying from the wrong revision is a costly and common error. Revision C is normally the latest, but the owner may have asked for changes, so confirm with the designer which drawing is current before committing the firm's money.

questions.q: What is Supplier A's total for the 120 panels, after its discount and before GCT?
questions.why: 120 × J$6 800 = J$816 000. The 5% discount is J$40 800, leaving J$775 200. J$734 400 takes off 10% instead of 5%, and J$856 800 adds the 5% instead of taking it off.

questions.q: What must Tamara do before she compares the prices of A and B?
o: Take B's price as it is, because it already includes GCT
Put both on the same GCT basis and add any delivery charge
Compare only unit prices, as delivery is a small part of it
Ask A to quote including GCT, so that it matches B's quote
questions.why: B's price includes GCT and A's does not, and B charges for delivery. Comparing them as they stand makes B look dearer or cheaper than it really is. Put every offer on the same basis, with discounts off and delivery added, then compare.

questions.q: Why is Supplier C's offer unsuitable, even though it is the cheapest?
o: It is too late for the job and shows no certification
Its price is 'all in', which a firm may not accept
Only approved suppliers are allowed to offer warranties
Its price is so low that GCT cannot be charged on it
questions.why: The panels are needed in 4 weeks and C needs 6, and an uncertified fitting may be unsafe and fail inspection. Being off the approved list is a further concern, but lateness and doubtful quality are what make it poor value here.

questions.q: B's sales representative phones Tamara and asks what A quoted, so that B can 'beat it'. What should she do?
o: Tell him, since a lower price saves the school money
Give him a rough figure, but not A's exact quotation
Keep A's price private and treat both suppliers alike
Tell him A's price, but only if B's offer is better
questions.why: Quotations are given in confidence. Passing one supplier's price to another is unfair and soon stops honest suppliers quoting. If a better price is wanted, ask every supplier for its best offer on the same terms at the same time.

questions.q: Tanisha works out 18 500 × 157 = J$2 904 500. Why is this not the full amount to budget for the board?
o: GCT is never charged on goods brought into Jamaica
The exchange rate is fixed once the order has been placed
The US$ price always includes delivery to the site
Freight, duty, import taxes and fees are still to be added
questions.why: J$2 904 500 is only the supplier's price converted. The landed cost also includes freight and insurance, customs duty and import taxes (including GCT on imports), broker and port charges and local delivery. The exchange rate can also move before payment.

questions.q: At the latest, when must the switchboard be ordered?
o: In week 1, when the job starts on site
At least 3 weeks before the job starts
By week 3, before first fix is finished
In week 8, one week before it is needed
questions.why: Work back from week 9: 10 weeks' lead time, 1 week for customs and 1 week's margin is 12 weeks. 9 − 12 = week −3, so the order must go in at least 3 weeks before the job begins.

questions.q: The supplier offers to send two pro forma invoices, each for half the board, so that both fall under Tanisha's limit. What should she do?
o: Accept, since each invoice is then within her own limit
Accept, but tell the contracts manager after it is paid
Refuse; the whole order needs the contracts manager's approval
Refuse, and order the board from a local supplier instead
questions.why: Splitting one purchase to get under an approval limit defeats the control that the limit provides, and auditors look for it. The board is one purchase of well over J$1 500 000, so it goes to the contracts manager.

questions.q: What should Omari write on the delivery note before he signs it?
o: Nothing, if he reports the problems to the office later
Received in good order, as the driver must leave now
One roll is 12 AWG, not 10 AWG; 38 breakers, 2 short
Short delivery, with details to follow from the office
questions.why: A signed note with no comment says the goods arrived correct. Write each problem clearly and exactly before signing, so that the supplier cannot dispute it later. A vague 'details to follow' gives the supplier room to argue.

questions.q: The site electrician says the 12 AWG roll can be used on the 30 A circuits, as those runs are short. What should Omari do?
o: Let him use it, as short runs carry the load safely
Use it, but fit 20 A breakers on those circuits instead
Keep it for the lighting circuits and order no more 10 AWG
Tag it, keep it apart, and return it for the 10 AWG ordered
questions.why: 12 AWG copper is normally protected at no more than 20 A, so on a 30 A circuit it could overheat whatever the run length. Changing the breakers changes the design. The roll is a wrong item: tag it, keep it apart and have it exchanged.

questions.q: What should happen about the solvent cement with no safety data sheet?
o: Get the SDS from the supplier before the cement is used
Use it, as the warning on the tin gives the same details
Return all four tins, since they cannot be used at all now
Use it outdoors only, until the SDS is sent by the supplier
questions.why: The SDS gives the hazards, safe storage, PPE, first aid and spill action that the short label on the tin does not. Suppliers can usually send it at once. Until then, store the tins closed, away from heat and sparks, in a ventilated place.

questions.q: Two weeks later the invoice charges for 6 rolls of 10 AWG and 40 breakers, at higher prices than the order. What should the office do?
o: Pay it in full, then claim the difference back later
Pay it, because Omari signed for the delivery
Refuse to pay any of it until the next order
Query it, and pay for accepted goods at order prices
questions.why: The order, the goods-received record and the invoice must agree before payment. Only 5 correct rolls and 38 breakers were accepted, at the PO prices. Query the difference, get a corrected invoice or credit note, and pay what is truly owed.

questions.q: At what stock balance should Sanya reorder the 20 A breakers?
questions.why: Reorder level = usage during the lead time + safety stock = 9 × 3 + 10 = 37. 27 leaves out the safety stock, and 19 counts only one week of use.

questions.q: The count shows 31 breakers but the stock card shows 36. What should Sanya do first?
o: Change the card to 31 so that it matches the shelf
Recount, then check recent issues and job cards
Order 5 more breakers to bring the stock back up
Tell the storemen that they will pay for the five
questions.why: A difference may be a counting error, an issue not written down, a wrong entry, damage or theft. Recount, then trace recent issues and job cards to find the cause. Correct the record only with approval, and fix whatever caused the gap.

questions.q: What is the best action on the drum of 6 AWG cable?
o: Stop the automatic reorder and plan to use, return or sell it
Keep reordering it, as a large drum is cheaper per metre
Move it to the back of the store to make room for new stock
Cut it into short lengths so that it will sell faster
questions.why: A slow-moving item ties up money and space, and its sheath ages. Stop reordering it, offer it for suitable jobs, or return or sell it. Buying in bulk only saves money when the stock is actually used.

questions.q: A quotation dated 2 May says 'valid 30 days'. The firm wants to order at those prices on 12 June. What should the purchaser do first?
o: Order at once, since the supplier has already agreed the prices
Ask the supplier to confirm the prices, as the quotation has expired
Order at the old prices and then pay whatever the invoice says
Add 10% to every line to allow for price rises since May
questions.why: A quotation binds the supplier only for its stated time. By 12 June it has expired, so the prices may have changed. Get them confirmed, or a new quotation, before raising the order, so that the order and the invoice will agree.

questions.q: Why do many firms make sure the person who places orders is not the person who approves payments to suppliers?
o: Errors and fraud are much harder to hide
Suppliers are paid more quickly that way
It means fewer quotations are needed
One person cannot learn both of those jobs
questions.why: When one person can both order and pay, they could pay for goods that never came, or favour a supplier, without anyone noticing. Keeping the duties apart means a second person checks the three-way match before money leaves the firm.
